title: Scrambled Eggs with Smoked Salmon
subtitle: Creamy, slow-cooked scrambled eggs with ribbons of smoked salmon
excerpt: Slow scrambled eggs are a different thing entirely from the fast kind, soft, barely-set curds with a silky texture that holds a ribbon of smoked salmon together without competing with it.
sourceNotes: Scrambled eggs with smoked salmon is a long-standing British celebration breakfast, particularly associated with weekend and holiday mornings. The slow low-heat technique is the standard professional method.

glossaryTerms.definition: When scrambled eggs seize and separate into dry, rubbery grains because the heat was too high or they were left too long without stirring, the proteins contract and expel liquid instead of setting into soft, cohesive curds.

content.text: Slow scrambled eggs are soft, barely-set curds that coat the palate rather than filling the mouth with dry, rubbery chunks. The technique is counterintuitive, low heat, constant movement, and pulling the pan off the flame before the eggs look done. Smoked salmon added off the heat keeps its silky texture and cool contrast against the warm eggs. The combination is rich enough to feel like a treat and simple enough to make on a weekday morning once the method is in your hands.

Crack the {{eggs}} eggs into a bowl and add the {{double-cream}} double cream. Beat lightly with a fork, just enough to break the yolks and combine them with the whites. Do not whisk aggressively; you are not trying to incorporate air. Season with a small pinch of {{sea-salt-flakes}} sea salt flakes and a little {{black-pepper}} black pepper. The cream is not there to make the eggs richer, it slows down the cooking by diluting the proteins slightly, giving you more time to control the texture.

Put a small saucepan or milk pan over the lowest heat your hob will give you and add the {{unsalted-butter}} butter. Let it melt without foaming. Pour in the egg mixture and begin stirring immediately with a silicone spatula, moving it in long sweeps across the base and sides of the pan. The key is constant, gentle motion, you are encouraging the eggs to set in small, soft layers rather than letting them sit and firm up in one mass. After three to four minutes, small, glossy curds will begin to form. The moment the eggs look barely-set and still slightly underdone, pull the pan off the heat entirely and keep stirring for another thirty seconds. Residual heat will finish them.

Once the pan is off the heat and the eggs are done, fold in the {{smoked-salmon}} smoked salmon, torn into rough ribbons rather than neat strips, so it distributes through the curds rather than sitting on top. The warmth of the eggs is enough to soften the salmon without cooking it. Scatter most of the {{chives}} chives in now and fold through. Taste and adjust the seasoning: smoked salmon is already salty, so you may not need any extra salt at all.
The thing to avoid at every stage is letting the eggs

. This happens when the heat is too high, the stirring stops, or the eggs stay in the pan after they are set. The result is grainy, watery, and unpleasant, nothing like the soft, cohesive curds you are after. If you see the eggs seizing quickly and turning rubbery, take the pan off the heat immediately and stir vigorously to arrest the cooking.

Spoon onto thick slices of toasted brown bread or sourdough. The toast should be ready and waiting before the eggs go into the pan, scrambled eggs do not hold. Scatter the remaining chives over the top. A wedge of lemon on the side is a small thing that lifts the whole plate: a squeeze over the salmon just before eating brightens the richness considerably.
Eggs are watery and separated: the heat was too high and the eggs curdled. There is no fixing them at this point. Start again on a lower heat, stirring from the moment the eggs go in.

Eggs are too firm and dry: you left them in the pan too long. Pull them off earlier, they should look slightly underdone when you take the pan off the heat, because the residual heat carries them the rest of the way.
Salmon has cooked and turned opaque: the eggs were too hot when the salmon went in. Let the pan cool for a minute off the heat before folding in the salmon.
